claims.statement: In 5-15% of patients with isolated colonic involvement, it may not be possible initially to distinguish between ulcerative colitis or CD; these patients are given a diagnosis of IBD-unclassified (IBDU). Before making an IBDU determination, evaluation of these patients should include careful clinical, radiographic, colonoscopic, and histological assessment for features more typical for CD.
claims.evidence_excerpt: Features favoring CD in indeterminate colitis: family history of CD, nonbloody diarrhea and weight loss at presentation, patchy inflammation or rectal sparing on endoscopy/histology, serological markers (ASCA+/pANCA-). claims.statement: Because of low sensitivity, screening for IBD in the general population is not appropriate... serological testing is insufficiently sensitive and specific to accurately diagnose IBD independent of clinical, endoscopic, and histological criteria.
claims.evidence_excerpt: IBD-associated antibodies (ASCA IgA/IgG, anti-OmpC, anti-CBir1, anti-I2) have >90% specificity but low sensitivity for distinguishing IBD from non-IBD. claims.statement: The clinical presentation of patients with CD is diverse and heterogeneous, with symptoms that can range from silent, insidious progression of mid-small bowel inflammation that might be misdiagnosed for years as 'irritable bowel syndrome' to a more acute presentation of diarrhea and/or weight loss, GI hemorrhage, perianal abscess/fistula, or intestinal obstruction.
claims.evidence_excerpt: Disease distribution: terminal ileum most common (60% have at least some ileal involvement); about half of ileal patients also have colonic involvement (usually right colon); ~20% isolated colonic involvement; ~30% confined to small bowel; ~5% upper tract (esophagus, stomach, duodenum, jejunum). claims.statement: Colonoscopy with ileal intubation is generally required for the assessment of CD and should include biopsies for histopathology assessment to exclude infection and lymphoma and corroborate the severity of inflammation... Noncaseating granulomata are considered pathognomonic for CD in this setting, although they are seen in only about 15% of patients with CD.
claims.evidence_excerpt: Endoscopic findings: erythema, erosions, ulcerations (classified as aphthous, linear, stellate, or serpiginous), strictures. claims.statement: Cross-sectional imaging modalities (CT and magnetic resonance imaging) with enterography protocols have largely replaced small bowel follow-through for the routine evaluation of known and suspected CD. These modalities are first-line imaging techniques that can rapidly and accurately identify areas of mucosal inflammation, fibrostenotic and penetrating complications, and many EIMs of CD.
claims.evidence_excerpt: CTE advantages: rapid image acquisition, lower cost, high accuracy for small bowel inflammation. claims.statement: Diagnosis of ulcerative colitis is based on clinical, endoscopic, and histological findings. In a patient with symptoms suggestive of ulcerative colitis (rectal bleeding, diarrhea and/or urgency), the diagnostic approach typically involves laboratory tests (serum and stool), endoscopy, and histology.
claims.evidence_excerpt: The chapter structures the diagnostic approach around this triad. Laboratory investigations (CBC, liver enzymes, albumin, CRP/ESR) assess inflammatory burden and complications but are not diagnostic. Stool testing rules out infection. claims.statement: The diagnostic performance of these serological tests is suboptimal and they should not used to screen for, or diagnose, ulcerative colitis (or Crohn's disease).
claims.evidence_excerpt: pANCA is present in 50-80% of UC patients but also in up to 31% of CD patients (especially colonic CD with UC-like endoscopic appearance). claims.statement: The disease presents as diffuse, continuous inflammation beginning in the rectum, with proximal extension that varies among individual patients. For initial evaluation, however, it is advisable to perform a full colonoscopy with ileal examination, to rule out Crohn's disease and to determine the proximal margin of disease.
claims.evidence_excerpt: Table 63.1 (adapted from Hogan et al. 1980) provides a specificity index for endoscopic features distinguishing UC from CD. claims.statement: A metaanalysis of 2499 patients observed a pooled sensitivity and specificity of 49% and 92% for C-reactive protein, and 88% and 73% for fecal calprotectin in IBD. Fecal calprotectin is a more sensitive biomarker of mucosal inflammation than C-reactive protein, and is more sensitive in ulcerative colitis compared to Crohn's disease.
claims.evidence_excerpt: The 2,499-patient meta-analysis (Mosli et al. 2015) provides pooled test characteristics. claims.statement: Microbiological testing using stool cultures for bacterial pathogens, panel-based nucleic acid amplification tests for potential bacterial, viral, and parasitic pathogens and, most importantly, polymerase chain reaction for Clostridium difficile toxin are indicated in all patients with diarrhea with suspected ulcerative colitis.
claims.evidence_excerpt: Approximately 10-15% of UC patients with diarrhea test positive for C. difficile, and another 15-20% may test positive for other organisms. claims.statement: The Montreal classification includes age at diagnosis, disease location, and the presence of perianal disease and is the most recognized CD classification in clinical research.
claims.evidence_excerpt: Montreal Classification components: Age (A1 <16, A2 17-40, A3 >40), Location (L1 ileal, L2 colonic, L3 ileocolonic, L4 isolated upper disease [modifier added to L1-L3]), Behavior (B1 non-stricturing non-penetrating, B2 stricturing, B3 penetrating), with "p" modifier for perianal disease. claims.statement: For all patients with ulcerative colitis, two aspects are vital for decision making: disease activity assessment, which is the cross-sectional assessment of symptomatic and endoscopic activity at that time point, and disease severity assessment, which involves evaluating the longitudinal disease course and prognosticating patients as being at low or high risk of complications.
claims.evidence_excerpt: The Mayo Clinic score is the most widely used activity index, incorporating stool frequency (0-3), rectal bleeding (0-3), physician global assessment (0-3), and endoscopic subscore (0-3). claims.statement: Ulcerative colitis should be considered in any patient who presents with rectal bleeding or chronic diarrhea... The most common problem in the differential diagnosis of an acute presentation of ulcerative colitis (including flare-ups of quiescent disease) is ruling out infectious colitis.

claims.statement: While there are no pathognomonic histological criteria for the diagnosis of ulcerative colitis, a primary distinction between ulcerative colitis and acute self-limited (infectious) colitis is architectural distortion.
claims.evidence_excerpt: In UC, the normal vertical ("test tube") alignment of glands is distorted, branched, and irregularly shaped.
